notes.18:21: Literally "limp on both knee-joints," a vivid Greek idiom (vs. Hebrew MT "between two opinions/branches"); similarly in v. 27 the Greek renders Elijah's taunt as "occupied in conversation" and "transacting business."
notes.18:32: Literally "a sea" (also in vv. 35 and 38), the Greek term for the water trench or basin around the altar.
notes.18:45: The Greek reads "wept" (vs. Hebrew MT "rode") and "to Israel" here and in v. 46 (where the Hebrew MT has "to Jezreel"); in v. 44 the Greek likewise reads "the footprint of a man, bringing up water" (vs. MT "a man's palm, rising from the sea").
notes.19:2: The Greek opens Jezebel's oath with the distinctive clause 'If you are Elijah and I am Jezebel' (absent in the Hebrew Masoretic Text) and uses singular 'God' with a positive oath statement introduced by hoti ('that').
notes.19:4: 'broom bush' renders the Greek transliteration rathmen (from Hebrew rotem, a desert broom shrub), whereas v. 5 uses the general Greek noun phyton ('plant'); in v. 3 the Greek also reads 'was afraid' (ephobethe) rather than Hebrew 'saw.'
notes.19:11: This Greek text reads en to pneumati Kyriou ('in the wind of the Lord') without the negation 'not' that appears in the following clauses and in the Hebrew text ('the Lord was not in the wind').
notes.19:16: The Greek reads 'the son of Jehu, son of Nimshi' rather than Hebrew 'Jehu son of Nimshi,' and in v. 18 likewise has second-person 'you will leave' (kataleipseis) rather than first-person 'I will leave.'
notes.19:20: The Greek omits 'and my mother' and renders Elijah's reply as a statement, Anastrephe, hoti pepoieka soi ('Return, for I have done it to you'), without the interrogative 'what' of the Hebrew text.
notes.20:1: In the Septuagint, the Naboth narrative stands as chapter 20 (corresponding to Hebrew 1 Kings 21). Throughout this chapter the Greek consistently calls Naboth 'the Israelite' (rather than Hebrew 'the Jezreelite'), places his vineyard beside Ahab's 'threshing floor' (halo, rather than 'palace'), and in v. 23 reads 'the outer wall of Israel' (rather than 'of Jezreel').
notes.20:10: This Greek text ends after 'sons of lawless men,' omitting the rest of Jezebel's written instructions about accusing and stoning Naboth; in v. 13 it uses second-person Heulogekas ('You have blessed,' a traditional euphemism for 'cursed').
notes.20:16: The Greek includes an additional notice that Ahab tore his garments and put on sackcloth upon hearing of Naboth's death before going down to take the vineyard (cf. v. 27).
notes.20:19: Rather than a question, the Greek begins with a causal statement ('Since you have murdered...'), includes 'the swine' alongside the dogs in 'every place,' and adds the prophecy that the prostitutes will wash themselves in Ahab's blood.
notes.20:25: The Greek reads plen mataios Achaab ('Yet in vain was Ahab') where the Hebrew has 'Surely there was none like Ahab,' and in v. 27 describes Ahab as 'stricken with remorse' (katenyge, also v. 29) and putting on sackcloth on the day he struck down Naboth.
notes.21:1: In the Septuagint, 3 Kingdoms 21 corresponds to 1 Kings 20 in the Hebrew Bible. The Greek renders the Aramean royal name Ben-hadad literally as "Son of Hader" (υἱὸς Ἁδέρ, reflecting an r/d interchange).
notes.21:10: The Greek reads "for the foxes" (ταῖς ἀλώπεξιν), interpreting the unvocalized Hebrew consonants for "handfuls" (lish'alim) as "foxes" (shu'alim), and renders "those at my feet" as "my foot soldiers."
notes.21:11: Where the Hebrew proverb contrasts strapping on armor with taking it off, the Greek renders the saying as a contrast between a "hunchbacked man" (ὁ κυρτός) and an "upright man" (ὁ ὀρθός).
notes.21:18: Verses 18-19 present a difficult Greek text with infinitives of command (εἰπεῖν, συλλαβεῖν), the clause "for they are not coming out" (οὐ γὰρ ἐκπορεύονται), and a prohibition in v. 19 ("let not ... come out," μὴ ἐξελθάτωσαν) where the Hebrew shifts to narrative.
notes.21:40: The Greek diverges sharply from the Hebrew verdict ("So shall your judgment be; you yourself have decided it"), reading "the ambushes with me" (τὰ ἔνεδρα παρ᾽ ἐμοί) and rendering the verb as "you have murdered" (ἐφόνευσας).
notes.22:8: Jemias (Greek Iemias, genitive Iemia in v. 9) preserves the Septuagint name form where the Hebrew text reads Imlah.
notes.22:16: The Greek text reads "Five times" (pentakis) as a statement, whereas the Hebrew asks "How many times?" (and some Greek manuscripts read posakis).
notes.22:17: The Greek renders this clause as a question, "Is the Lord not God to these?", contrasting with the Hebrew "These have no master."
notes.22:24: The Greek literally reads Canaan (Chanaan, compared to Chaana for Hebrew Chenaanah in v. 11) and asks "What kind of spirit of the Lord is it that spoke in you?" rather than the Hebrew "Which way did the Spirit of the Lord go from me to speak to you?"
notes.22:26: The Greek names the official Semer and titles him "the king of the city," where the Hebrew text has Amon the governor of the city.
notes.22:42: The Greek names Jehoshaphat's maternal grandfather Shimei (Semeei) where the Hebrew has Shilhi; verses 47-50 do not appear here in the Septuagint order (parallel material stands earlier in 16:28a-h).

unplaced.note: The Saints Greek Critical Text has this sentence as 4:33 at the end of chapter 4; it has no separate place in the Saints.Bible numbering, so it is shown after 4:19.
